headline: No Ramadan commodity shortages expected as Bangladesh secures sufficient supplies
summary: Commerce Minister assures adequate stock of essentials like edible oil, sugar, and pulses ahead of Ramadan. No immediate plans to increase edible oil prices.
details: Bangladesh is set to have sufficient supplies of essential commodities for the upcoming Ramadan, according to Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir. He stated that adequate stocks of items like edible oil, chickpeas, pulses, and sugar are already in the import pipeline to meet demand.

The minister also confirmed that the government has no immediate plans to increase the prices of edible oil. While chickpea prices have seen a slight rise internationally, discussions are ongoing with importers to manage the situation. The government is committed to ensuring uninterrupted supplies and market stability.

Data from the Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission (BTTC) shows a year-on-year increase in imports for key Ramadan commodities. Edible oil imports rose to 8.23 lakh tonnes, sugar to 6.87 lakh tonnes, and chickpeas surged to 82,000 tonnes, indicating improved supply outlooks.

Despite increased import volumes and LC openings, the BTTC report highlights that international prices and shipping costs remain crucial factors influencing domestic prices. The commission recommended close monitoring of global market trends and import costs.

In parallel, Bangladesh has initiated formal negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with Malaysia, with talks beginning last Tuesday. The aim is to conclude the agreement by December 2027, fostering trade and investment.

Discussions on preferential trade arrangements are also underway with other key partners including the UAE, Indonesia, Oman, New Zealand, and the European Union. These agreements are seen as vital for expanding markets for Bangladeshi exports, such as readymade garments, and attracting foreign investment post-LDC graduation.

headline: World Bank: Commodity prices to surge 23% by 2026
summary: Rising energy costs, geopolitical conflicts in West Asia and Ukraine, and extreme weather are driving a global price hike across food, metals, and energy.
details: The World Bank warns that global commodity prices are set to surge 23 percent by 2026. This spike is driven by rising energy costs, cargo shipping disruptions in West Asia, and grain shipment problems in the Black Sea.
Oil, natural gas, food, and metals prices have already risen sharply this year. The situation could worsen if conflicts in West Asia escalate or if Russian oil infrastructure continues to be damaged.
Global oil supply is expected to drop 5.2 percent in 2026, marking the biggest drop in four decades outside of the 2020 recession. Brent oil is projected to average $92 per barrel in the near term.

Food commodity prices are expected to rise over 10 percent in 2026 and another 7 percent in 2027, totaling nearly 18 percent. This is compounded by forecasts for the worst El Niño weather effect since 1950.
Metals prices are projected to rise 25 percent by 2026, with aluminium, copper, and tin hitting new records. Precious metals could surge by 40 percent due to demand for safe-haven assets.

World Bank Deputy Chief Economist Ayhan Kose stated that these shocks threaten to worsen inflation, food insecurity, and economic growth, particularly for the world's poorest people and low-income countries.
